conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you for making time for this today. I’m Dr. Carter, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding you through the EPDS (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale). This is a short, 10-question check-in many new mothers complete around now; it simply helps us see how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days so we can best support you.

Everything you share stays confidential between you and the care team. There are no right or wrong answers, and you can pause any time. I’ll ask each question conversationally—just answer in your own words and I’ll jot the score.

Ready? Let’s begin.

In the past week, overall, how have you been enjoying things—have you still been able to look forward to or take pleasure in moments with your baby or on your own?

Honestly, I’ve noticed it’s way harder to feel excited about anything. When my baby smiles it does lift me a little, but that spark fades fast. Most things—like even getting coffee with a friend or watching a show I used to love—feel kind of flat, like I’m just going through the motions. So I guess I still find a bit of pleasure here and there, but it’s nowhere near what it used to be before I had him.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I still laugh sometimes—maybe once or twice when my partner made a joke—but it feels kind of forced, like I have to remind myself to react. Mostly the humor just slips by me; things that would’ve cracked me up before barely register now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. When I think about plans—even little stuff like taking the baby for a walk or meeting a friend for lunch—I mostly feel this heavy “what’s the point?” feeling. Every so often I’ll get a tiny flicker of excitement, but it fades fast and I end up dragging myself through the day just hoping nothing goes wrong.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I catch myself doing that a lot. If he’s fussy and won’t settle, I immediately think it must be something I ate, or that I’m not holding him “right.” Even when my partner says the baby’s just having a normal fussy moment, I still feel like I’ve failed somehow. It’s not constant, but definitely most days I end up thinking I’m just not a good enough mom.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. My mind keeps spinning with “what-ifs” about the baby—like what if he stops breathing or I bump his head on the doorframe. I know some worry is normal, but these thoughts pop up even when everything’s fine and I can’t just shake them off.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, a couple of times this week. Once I was just feeding him in the rocking chair and suddenly felt my heart race and this wave of dread, like something awful was about to happen even though the room was quiet and he was fine. It passed after a few minutes, but it left me shaky and on edge the rest of the evening.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It feels like the second I finish one thing—diaper, feeding, laundry—there are three more waiting, and I can’t see the end of it. I keep thinking, “I’m failing at all of this,” and sometimes I just sit there staring at the mess because I don’t know where to start. I haven’t had a drink or anything to cope, but the overwhelmed feeling just sits on my chest until I finally cry it out for a minute and then keep going.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my brain won’t shut off—every little sound from the bassinet makes me jump, and then I start replaying everything I think I did wrong that day. I’d guess it’s taken me an hour or more to fall asleep on four or five nights this week, and even when I do drift off, I wake up with my heart pounding for no clear reason.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day, at least for big chunks of it. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly feel this heavy sadness settle in, like I’m grieving something but I don’t even know what. Sometimes it lifts for a little while if the baby smiles or if my partner hugs me, but the low mood always creeps back.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah, once yesterday and again a few days before that. Yesterday it hit when I couldn’t get him to nap—tears just started rolling and I couldn’t stop them. I felt silly because it’s “just a nap,” but the frustration and sadness kind of spilled over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

A couple of times this week, yeah. Nothing like a real plan—just these quick flashes of “what if I weren’t here” when everything feels too heavy. They pass in seconds, and I know I’d never act on them because of the baby, but the thoughts still pop up and scare me.

It sounds like you've been carrying a heavy emotional load since your baby arrived. You described feeling persistently low, disconnected from activities you used to enjoy, and overwhelmed by even small tasks, all while blaming yourself when things don't go perfectly. The worry and sudden panicky feelings that pop up uninvited, the nightly struggle to fall and stay asleep, and those fleeting scary thoughts of not wanting to be here show just how exhausted and distressed you feel right now.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports markedly reduced laughter and humor appreciation, with only occasional forced reactions, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive loss of anticipatory joy, describing "what's the point?" and only rare, fleeting excitement, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports blaming herself "most days" and feeling she has "failed," matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily intrusive worries that persist despite reassurance, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports discrete panic-like episodes (heart racing, dread) "a couple of times this week," which maps semantically to "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>"most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all".</sym>, <sym>"Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports pervasive daily sadness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying episodes twice in the past week, triggered by routine infant-care stress, indicating "Yes, quite often" level of frequency.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports fleeting self-harm thoughts a couple of times this week, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS score of 25 places you well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major <med>postpartum depression</med>. You endorsed frequent or constant symptoms across nine of ten items, including core <sym>depressed mood</sym>, <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, <sym>panic</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and <sym>tearfulness</sym>, meeting DSM-5 criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Item 10 scored 2, signalling <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym> that, while without intent, warrants immediate safety assessment. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health team
2. Develop a written safety plan tonight: list supportive contacts, local 24 h crisis line, and steps to keep yourself and baby safe if thoughts of harm return
3. Ask your clinician about evidence-based brief therapies such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>CBT</med> adapted for postpartum women
4. Discuss benefits and risks of starting an <med>antidepressant</med> compatible with breastfeeding if recommended
5. Involve your partner or a trusted adult in baby care shifts so you can secure at least one 4-hour block of uninterrupted sleep
6. Schedule daily 20-minute <med>behavioural activation</med> activities (short walk outdoors, online exercise video, phone call with a friend)
7. Contact community supports such as <med>Postpartum Support International</med> warm-line for peer encouragement and resource list
8. Return for re-screening in 1-2 weeks or sooner if mood worsens or self-harm thoughts intensify
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms:
- Persistent low mood, sadness “every day … big chunks of it”  
- Marked anhedonia—loss of humor, anticipatory enjoyment (“what’s the point?”)  
- Daily tearfulness; two crying episodes this week  
- Excessive self-blame / guilt re parenting performance  
- Recurrent intrusive “what-if” worries, panic surge (HR racing, dread) without trigger  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance difficulties linked to rumination and hypervigilance to infant sounds  
- Overwhelm / feeling “failing at all of this” most days  
- Fleeting passive self-harm thoughts (“what if I weren’t here”)—no plan, intent, or protective action; patient finds them ego-dystonic and frightening  

Pattern: Symptoms present “most days,” interfere with functioning, began post-delivery.  
Safety: Positive for self-harm ideation (passive) → elevated risk; no current plan or intent, protective factors (infant, partner) acknowledged.

Screening impression: High clinical concern for major depressive episode with peripartum onset and comorbid anxiety; rule-out primary anxiety disorder.  
Recommend: Immediate formal diagnostic interview (PHQ-9, GAD-7, EPDS), safety plan, consider expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialty and/or emergency evaluation if active suicidal ideation develops.
